content:
I've formalized a proof that for every choice of four positive masses and each cyclic order there is exactly one strictly convex planar central configuration, up to similarity. This was conjectured by Albouy, Fu and Sun in 2008 and is Problem 10 of Albouy, Cabral and Santos (2012). Preprint: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35632. Repo: https://github.com/tejasvi/lean4body

  • The statements are in C4/C4/Defs.lean, C4/C4/TheoremA.lean and C4/C4/TheoremB.lean, and C4/README.md lists them. #print axioms gives propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.
  • The interval arithmetic is a branch and bound written in Lean. It replays hints from an unverified search in 3418 decide +kernel certificates, with no native_decide. The certificates take about 19 minutes on 32 threads and the rest of the development about two minutes.
  • nanoda checks the 211 certificate files with only the standard axioms, and separately the rest of the development with the certificates as axioms. A script checks that the two parts fit together by comparing hashes.

I'd be grateful for eyes on the statement files especially whether they match with Theorem A?

Just to flag our community guidelines, which amongst other things state "This is not a free code review service." Also to flag the community norms about Lean code: for code to be accepted to a public Lean repository such as Palomar, it needs to satisfy certain requirements as specified here https://palomar-registry.org/about#what-registration-requires and your code does not (tl;dr: #comparator and #formalization.yaml )
Thanks for the pointers and apologies for the review request. I'll look at preparing the formalization for Palomar.

The uniqueness theorem is now registered on Palomar: PALOMAR-2026-10-02-000011

  • To fit Palomar's time and memory budget, the registered repository, https://github.com/tejasvi/lean4body-uniqueness, uses a weaker computer-assisted bound proof, without affecting the uniqueness result: Q ≥ K/128 in place of Theorem B's Q ≥ K/4. That is used by Theorem A to prove uniqueness. The Challenge.lean states Theorem A (three forms), nondegeneracy, and the count of three convex central configurations.
  • lean4body, which proves Theorem B with the constant 1/4 and cited by the paper, is now checked in public CI by Lean's kernel and nanoda, with con-ron also checking its certificate modules: https://github.com/tejasvi/lean4body-check/releases/tag/run-36935878734
